title: Kimi's New Race Engineer 'Giorgio' Was George Russell
description: George Russell hopped on Kimi Antonelli's radio posing as race engineer Giorgio. What happened, the Daft Punk joke, and the AI voice angle.
author: freellm.site
content:
If you searched for "Kimi speaking to his new race engineer Giorgio Russell," the short answer is that there's no engineer called Giorgio. During the rain-delayed 2026 Singapore Grand Prix weekend, George Russell got onto Kimi Antonelli's team radio pretending to be his new race engineer, and Antonelli, sitting in the car waiting for the rain to ease, took a while to work out who he was talking to. F1 journalist Chris Medland reported the exchange on [Bluesky](https://bsky.app/profile/chrismedlandf1.bsky.social/post/3mxj5bqulu22j), and it went straight to the top of r/formula1 because of one line: Antonelli's confused "Who is?"

![Kimi's New Race Engineer 'Giorgio' Was George Russell](/images/blog/kimi-antonelli-russell-radio-prank-ai/image-0.jpg)

## What happened

The setup was ordinary: rain, a delay, and a driver strapped into a car with nothing to do but listen to the radio. Russell took the chance to appear as a new voice on Antonelli's channel, introducing himself as the engineer and staying in character. Antonelli answered, chatted, and only gradually realised another driver was winding him up rather than his team briefing him.

Two details explain why the clip spread so fast:

- **"Who is?"** is a word-for-word carry-over of the Italian *chi è?*. In English you'd say "who is this?", but the Italian construction drops the object, and Antonelli's brain clearly stayed in Italian while his mouth switched to English. Italian speakers in the thread spotted it immediately, and plenty of non-Italian speakers said it was the most charming part.
- **The name.** Calling himself Giorgio handed the internet a free punchline, and the thread filled with variations on the spoken intro from Daft Punk's "Giorgio by Moroder": *my name is Giovanni Giorgio, but everybody calls me Giorgio.* Half the top comments on both threads riff on that line. One commenter escalated it to "driver-engineer-security guard Italian-Englishman Giorgio Rosselli."

Commenters also pointed out, correctly, that it's no knock on Antonelli that he didn't catch on instantly. Several said they didn't recognise Russell's voice in the clip either. Radio audio is compressed, band-limited and heavily clipped, and it throws away most of the timbre, which is what you actually use to recognise a familiar voice.

## Why nobody recognised the voice, and why that matters

Team radio carries roughly 300 Hz to 3.4 kHz of heavily compressed audio with engine and wind noise on top, delivered through an in-helmet earpiece. Remove the high frequencies from any voice and you remove most of what makes it identifiable. Add a put-on accent and a believable script (tyre temps, delay updates, "stay in the car") and context does the rest. Antonelli was *expecting* an engineer to talk to him about the rain, and Russell gave him exactly that.

Voice impersonation depends entirely on that gap between expecting a voice and verifying it, which is why a jokey F1 radio bit deserves a second look. Russell managed it with an accent and some nerve. Now anyone with a laptop can get the same effect.

## The uncomfortable version: synthetic race engineers

In 2026, the three pieces you'd need to build a convincing fake race engineer are all commodity products:

| Piece | What it does | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Speech-to-text | Transcribes what the driver says | Streaming models handle noisy, accented, clipped audio |
| An LLM | Generates terse, in-character engineer lines | A small fast model is better than a big slow one here |
| Text-to-speech / voice cloning | Speaks the output in a chosen voice | Quality varies wildly; check each vendor's consent policy |

The LLM is the cheapest and easiest part, and you can prototype it on a free tier today; see our roundup of the [best free LLM APIs in 2026](/blog/best-free-llm-apis-2026/) for current options. For anything involving voice, latency is the real constraint, because a radio reply that takes three seconds feels broken. That's why fast inference providers matter more than raw model quality for this kind of app; we compared them in [Groq vs Cerebras vs SambaNova](/blog/groq-vs-cerebras-vs-sambanova-free-tier/).

Voice cloning is where it stops being funny. A prank over team radio is consensual banter between colleagues. Cloning someone's voice to issue instructions they never gave is fraud, and the law on who answers for it is unsettled. We covered where things stand in [Who Is Liable When an AI Agent Breaks the Law?](/blog/who-is-liable-when-ai-agents-break-the-law/) and [FTC: AI Developers Liable for Their Agents' Conduct](/blog/ftc-ai-agent-liability-developers/).

## Build the harmless version

To get the Giorgio bit without the ethics problem, generate the *text* and read it out yourself. The prompt matters more than the model: real race engineers are extremely terse, and most LLMs will write a paragraph when you want nine words.

Here's a runnable example against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Swap the base URL and key for your free provider; see [What Is an OpenAI-Compatible API](/blog/openai-compatible-api-guide/) if the pattern is new to you.

```python
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url=os.environ["LLM_BASE_URL"],  # your provider's OpenAI-compatible URL
    api_key=os.environ["LLM_API_KEY"],
)

SYSTEM = """You are an F1 race engineer on team radio.
Rules:
- Maximum 12 words per message. Usually fewer.
- No greetings, no pleasantries, no explanations.
- Lead with the actionable word: Box, Push, Hold, Copy, Target.
- Never invent lap times, positions, or gaps. If unknown, say 'checking'.
- End with 'Copy?' only when you need confirmation."""

def radio(driver_says: str) -> str:
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=os.environ["LLM_MODEL"],
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
            {"role": "user", "content": driver_says},
        ],
        temperature=0.4,
        max_tokens=40,
    )
    return r.choices[0].message.content.strip()

for line in [
    "How long until we go? It's still raining.",
    "Who is?",
    "Tyres are cold, I can't feel the front.",
]:
    print(f"DRIVER: {line}")
    print(f"ENGINEER: {radio(line)}\n")
```

Three details matter. The `max_tokens=40` cap physically stops the model from rambling. The "never invent lap times" rule is there because models will happily make up a gap to the car ahead if you let them, which is the last thing you want in anything that looks like telemetry. And `temperature=0.4` keeps the replies clipped rather than creative.

To put this in a Discord server so your friends can talk to Giorgio, see [Build a Discord or Telegram Bot With a Free LLM API](/blog/free-llm-api-discord-telegram-bot/). Watch your rate limits if more than a couple of people use it at once, since [free tier limits vary a lot by provider](/blog/free-llm-api-rate-limits-compared/).

## The championship subtext

Part of why the clip landed so hard is where both drivers sit in the 2026 season. The surrounding Reddit threads were full of fans doing standings arithmetic, including a long hypothetical about the title picture if late-season rounds were cancelled, and plenty of commentary about Russell's own position in the table. None of that is settled: it was fan speculation on a Saturday, and the person who posted it framed it explicitly as hypothetical. For actual standings, go to the official F1 site instead of trusting a Reddit edit.

The tone, though, was clear. A recurring comment across both threads was relief that drivers at the front of the grid still mess with each other for fun. One reply summed up Antonelli as, unfortunately, a cinnamon roll. Some fans hoped Russell has more shithousery in him for wet races and next season, which seems a reasonable bet given he pulled this one off from a stationary car in the rain.

## FAQ

### Who is Giorgio, Kimi Antonelli's new race engineer?

Nobody. Giorgio was George Russell doing a bit on Antonelli's team radio during the rain delay at the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix. Antonelli's actual engineer hasn't changed; check Mercedes' own channels for personnel.

### Why did Kimi Antonelli say "Who is?"

It's a direct translation of the Italian *chi è?*, which leaves out the object English requires. He was thinking in Italian and speaking in English, which is why the line charmed the thread instead of reading as a mistake.

### What is the Daft Punk connection?

The name Giorgio set off mass quoting of the spoken intro to "Giorgio by Moroder," where Giorgio Moroder says his name is Giovanni Giorgio but everybody calls him Giorgio. It accounts for a large share of the top replies on both Reddit threads.

### Could an AI have faked that radio call?

Technically, yes. Streaming transcription, a fast LLM and modern text-to-speech are all commodity products in 2026, and radio audio is compressed enough to hide a lot of imperfection. Doing it with a real person's cloned voice without consent is a different matter, legally and ethically; see our pieces on [AI agent accountability](/blog/who-is-accountable-ai-agent-crime/).

### What model should I use to build a race-engineer chatbot?

Prioritise latency over size: for anything involving voice, a fast small model beats a slow large one. Start on a free tier from the [no-credit-card list](/blog/how-to-get-free-llm-api-key-no-credit-card/), test with your own prompt, and check each provider's official docs for current context limits and rate caps instead of trusting third-party tables.
